name: Ancient Ligurian

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls in Ancient Ligurian. The only accent-related claim in the accessible literature is de Bernardo Stempel's reconstruction that the Ligurian onomastic change *yo > (y)e (Blustiemelo, Lebriemelum, Nitielium, Berigiema) affected UNACCENTED *-yo-, with the accent placed earlier in the word (her *Bérgioma). This is a hypothesised accent condition on a sound change in reconstructed names under her Celtic-Ligurian hypothesis, not a description of a stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the language is known only from names and glosses.
new_statements.domain_note: Reconstructed proto-forms of place/tribal names transmitted in Latin texts (Sententia Minuciorum, CIL V 7749); no attested prosody, no word-vs-phrase domain applicable.
new_statements.identity_note: Ancient Ligurian (anci1248, xlg) is a fragmentarily attested pre-Roman language of Liguria/NW Italy known only from names, glosses and a few disputed inscriptions; some scholars (de Bernardo Stempel, Delamarre) treat the Indo-European layer as a Celtic ('Celto-Ligurian') dialect, others (Kretschmer, Falileyev, Mees) as a separate IE language. Not to be confused with modern Ligurian (Romance, ligu1248).

sources.quote: - montem Berigiemam, from a nominative *Bérgioma, i.e. *bhergh-yo-mā 'the highest' with West-Celtic epenthetic vowel in the second syllable and an equally archaic superlative suffix [...] It is therefore possible to recognize the change of unstressed yo to (y)e as a Celtic isogloss, and even to compare it with what happened later on in Goidelic
sources.locator: pp. 46-47 (§1 '*yo > ye in Ligurian onomastics', §2 'The Celto-Ligurian dialect'); cf. p. 49
sources.note: §1-2 (pp. 45-47): the recurrent Ligurian onomastic change *yo > (y)e (Devoto, Lejeune) is framed as 'the change of unstressed yo to (y)e' and treated as a Celtic isogloss; montem Berigiemam is reconstructed as *Bérgioma with an initial accent mark (p. 46); p. 49: 'Celto-Ligurian unaccented e < *yo'. This is an accent condition assumed for a reconstructed sound change in names under a Celtic hypothesis, not a description of where stress falls in the language.

sources.citation: Kretschmer, Paul. 1905. "Die Inschriften von Ornavasso und die ligurische Sprache." Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung 38: 97-128.
sources.note: Public-domain scanned of the whole article (pp. 97-128) read; discusses the Ornavasso/Lugano inscriptions, Ligurian ethnography, names, suffixes -asco/-asca, IE affiliation and some sound correspondences. No occurrence of Akzent/Betonung/betont/tonlos anywhere in the article.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en). "Ligurian language (ancient)" (raw wikitext fetched sources 2026-09-17); Wikipedia (it). "Lingua ligure antica"
sources.note: Used only as a bibliography index. Phonology paragraph (after Falileyev 2020) mentions 'unstressed *-i̯o- developed to -i̯e-' and reports Mees 2024 objecting that a Celtic reading requires 'unstressed *o > a'; no statement of stress position. Italian page: 'accento' does not occur.

sources.citation: Falileyev, Alexander. 2020. "The Silent Europe." Palaeohispanica 20: 887-919. DOI 10.36707/palaeohispanica.v0i20.372
sources.note: Section 2 (pp. 891-895) surveys the 'Ligurian' onomastic complex and on p. 895 summarises the historical phonetics of Indo-European Ligurian (centum; *bh > b, deaspiration; initial *p- and sonorants kept; most vowels kept, *o sporadically; *u > o in some positions; *yo > ye; suffixes -ink-, -isk-, -l-, -jo-, -ask-). Nothing on accent or stress; the only 'stress' hits are the verb 'stressed' in citations.

sources.citation: Mees, Bernard. 2024. "Ligurian and Lepontic: the inscriptions from Lunigiana and the Prestino stone." In C. Salomon & D. Stifter (eds.), Cisalpine Celtic Literacy. Proceedings of the International Symposium Maynooth 23-24 June 2022, 201-231. Berlin: Curach Bhán.
